## Design

### 2026-10-23 – Turns out I bit off a lot more than I could chew (who could've guessed?).

**2h**

Turns out I bit off a lot more than I could chew (who could've guessed?).
The original idea reel I made planned for the following components:
- 1x Waveshare ESP32-S3-Zero
- 4x Kailh Choc Low-Profile Switches
- 8x EC11 Rotary Encoders
- 2x Bourns Slide Potentiometers
- 12x Capacitive Touchpads

This was the approximate layout I had made:
![Old layout](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/WlipWVmF6UnTGNkVVXdowr37dB4xoM3o/a8d18bf916e22c233e29336c7d50525044fe97d94066a98410b07d49357c5b07.png)
Adding it up, all the components need **43** GPIO pins on the microcontroller. For context, the microcontroller I'm using (which I specifically chose so I'd have more GPIO) has 15 (usable) pins.

So, after a ton of research, reading datasheets, and counting pins, I scaled back my plan a bunch so I could still have a final outcome similar to what I wanted while keeping it actually practical. This is what the new, much more modest, approximate layout looks like:

![New layout](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/WlipWVmF6UnTGNkVVXdowr37dB4xoM3o/e7af2144fcf0b7ffa6ea7fdd935a0672542c848a714011f1cc67de03a2654b7d.png)

As you can see, the new design has:
- The same microcontroller
- The same number of touchpads
- 1 less key switch
- 1 less potentiometer
- 6 less rotary encoders

Most of the pin saving comes from the huge decrease in rotary encoders (those use 2 pins each, 3 if you want the switch functionality, which I do) and that extra chip you may have noticed.

That chip is a breakout board for the MPR121. While digging for methods to reduce my GPIO count, I stumbled across a discontinued chip that claims to serve the input of 12 capacitive pads over I2C (how convenient, that's exactly how many I need). The I2C connection only needs 4 pins (IRQ, SCL, SDA, and ADD), so all 12 pads can be hooked up to the microcontroller with only those 4 pins.

The actual MPR121 is a tiny 3mmx3mm QFN chip. That's why I need a breakout board to actually use it. The chip itself is technically discontinued, but there's still two main sources from which I can choose to buy the board.
- Adafruit makes a breakout board for the MPR121. It's well documented, easy to design around, and even has a bunch of QoL features like an LED indicator and a 3V regulator.
- There's also a generic-brand breakout board for the chip. It isn't well documented, and doesn't have most of the Adafruit board's benefits. *Except*, it's like 7 times cheaper.

I decided on the latter. This meant I had to make my own KiCAD symbol and footprint for the board and set it up in a library. Thankfully, I have some experience doing that and I was able to without much hassle. Hopefully this isn't foreshadowing.

That brings the total number of GPIO needed by my design down to exactly 15. Perfect. Now I'll begin designing the schematic for the board (my second favourite step!)

### 2026-10-23 – I created the schematic for the board in KiCad. While examining the pins on the MPR121 board, I realised I can actually save a GPIO pin by not wiring the ADD (address) pin. The pin is only needed if t

**1.52h**

I created the schematic for the board in KiCad. While examining the pins on the MPR121 board, I realised I can actually save a GPIO pin by not wiring the ADD (address) pin. The pin is only needed if the microcontroller is managing multiple I2C connections with the same SDA and SCL pins and the board I'm using already has a jumper tying the pin to GND, so it won't be floating. This meant I had one extra GPIO pin which I used to add another key switch to make it 4 in a grid (like the original plan). This also meant 4 LEDs instead of 3, one for each switch. Here is what the final schematic looks like:
![Schematic](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/WlipWVmF6UnTGNkVVXdowr37dB4xoM3o/2411edecbc1ffe73718614324370a5798971be996fdffc09c49c47d1a4c0468f.png)

I also designed the footprint for the capacitive pads. An octave worth of piano keys. Each white key is 20mm wide and each black key is 10mm wide. The minimum gap between adjacent pads is 2mm.

![Footprint](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/WlipWVmF6UnTGNkVVXdowr37dB4xoM3o/6717c060e22fef928f4f3696f8b4e44ae7066f4c560f549d60e85ffdd0d8c718.png)

[Timelapse](https://lookout.hackclub.com/api/media/b8cc3874-dbab-4f9f-8af9-5a81bb8937eb/video.mp4)

### 2026-10-23 – My favourite step: Laying out and routing the final PCB!

**2.52h**

My favourite step: Laying out and routing the final PCB!

First, I arranged all the components in the way I had planned, with precise locations this time. It ended up looking like this:
![Old layout](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/WlipWVmF6UnTGNkVVXdowr37dB4xoM3o/402399487a9dc292f0b88bad8edac28712dd8bb0eca8e47679437d76f8500b10.png)

Then, I started routing it, only to quickly realise the microcontroller's in a very annoying spot, right behind the key switches and so far from the rest of the components. So, I removed my old routing and reordered the components before routing again, much more neatly. I also modified the GPIO pins in the schematic a bit so the wiring would be slightly neater (I'm a bit of a perfectionist). Finally, it ended up looking like this:
![Routing](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/WlipWVmF6UnTGNkVVXdowr37dB4xoM3o/71b9237e637d82eb467dfd60819bac78da321a2e5ad8103d65adfd09e8c61894.png)

This final board completely passes the DRC. Next, I'll add some silkscreen graphics to the board and start sourcing parts.

### 2026-10-24 – First, I added silkscreen graphics to the board. Here's what the front and back now look like:

**2.28h**

First, I added silkscreen graphics to the board. Here's what the front and back now look like:

![Front](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/WlipWVmF6UnTGNkVVXdowr37dB4xoM3o/3f8f1ec22d7ab2b8a3cb1ab012c9ae0d837f3608f57b6ecbb3bdd8ebf9602ef2.png)

![Back](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/WlipWVmF6UnTGNkVVXdowr37dB4xoM3o/b50fcfa5a771e77a8c2bf15e0dfcbed310449db489cce4e6bcba9296e902cbe6.png)

Next, I created the BOM. This look *a while* because I had to find the cheapest source I could for each component, keeping shipping costs in mind too, while making sure the component I was looking at was actually the one my board was designed with. After reading [the guide](https://codex.hackclub.com/design/part-sourcing/) and doing a bunch of manual research, I managed to make a full list with each part:

![BOM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/WlipWVmF6UnTGNkVVXdowr37dB4xoM3o/c0654f6183340af98cbeb799de1c7e73c53f6fed093ee6c30a1df205778ea857.png)

Some things to mention:
- The PCB is way more expensive than usual (the board itself and JLCPCB's "engineering fee") because it's pretty big (168mmx113mm). I tried some other sites to get the PCB made, but they were all way more pricey.
- More than half of the shipping costs comes from DigiKey's shipping. I specifically tried to avoid it for that reason but it's really hard to find sources for the Bourns Potentiometer that don't have insanely high shipping.

I'm at the last stretch now so my goals are to write the whole firmware for the board (probably using KMK), learning how MIDI works along the way, hopefully optimise the BOM more so it's not crazy expensive, and write a detailed README for the project.

### 2026-10-25 – I made much bigger changes than I was expecting to today. After some consideration, I realised the Bourns Slider Potentiometer wasn't going to be very useful and definitely not worth the huge cost inc

**2.6h**

I made much bigger changes than I was expecting to today. After some consideration, I realised the Bourns Slider Potentiometer wasn't going to be very useful and definitely not worth the huge cost increase. So, I came up with some alternative layouts for the board I could use:

- Option A (4s2e1p): Same as the previous plan with 4 switches, 2 rotary encoders, and 1 potentiometer.
- Option B (6s2e0p): This version removes the potentiometer and uses the extra GPIO pin for two extra switches (one more is saved because the keys are wired in a 3x2 matrix* instead of individually)
- Option C (4s3e0p): This version uses the extra GPIO pin from removing the potentiometer to add a rotary encoder. It does this by, one, disconnecting the IRQ pin on the MPR121 breakout board (since that's technically not *needed* because the board can just poll the capacitive pads via I2C instead), and two, wiring up the key switches and the rotary encoder switches *together* as one big 2x4 matrix.

*I considered also adding a diode to each key so the matrix works consistently, even when multiple buttons are pressed, but decided against it because it's an unlikely requirement for this project and would add an unnecessary cost.

![Options A, B, and C](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/WlipWVmF6UnTGNkVVXdowr37dB4xoM3o/ae880b4d3e13eeaea11cdf2ca44f4299e6c09da53c1dfada6d752b93310a036d.png)

After some testing and research, I decided on Option B, because first of all, it's definitely better than Option A because two buttons are more useful than a slider, and of course, it's much cheaper. And secondly, It's much less cumbersome to route than Option C.

Although C would have the most utility, having to wire up the rotary encoder switches with the regular key switches all the way on the opposite side of the board in an weirdly shaped matrix would be very tedious and time consuming. Plus, the routing wouldn't be neat and tidy in the slightest. So since I'm reaching the deadline for this project, I decided on Option B.

So after the decision was made, I quickly modified the schematic and rearranged the PCB, making sure the spacing was still consistent, but with the new layout in mind. Then I rerouted the whole board for the new layout. I think this routing is even better than the previous iteration and I'm quite satisfied with it. Here's what the board looked like before and after.
![Old PCB](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/WlipWVmF6UnTGNkVVXdowr37dB4xoM3o/1bcb0862869f6c1eb354a9e56d705f3ec517953e90eab266797fdb73459c4e3e.png)

![New PCB](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/WlipWVmF6UnTGNkVVXdowr37dB4xoM3o/340ceb859c525b07e21660ddc092ef2c3afeae3f7cbe6638573e9ee10ef5789c.png)

Finally, I made the changes to the BOM I planned and I'm happy to say that it's now over 20% cheaper than the previous one:

![New BOM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/WlipWVmF6UnTGNkVVXdowr37dB4xoM3o/3e7a8c59f1ffbf9ba4bcad3d5f51681a56b4fe9dd8fe68254f17e8fc31e3c5e6.png)
